title: Syntax and Test Harness: Prompt Corpus & Regression Notes
body:
Purpose:
This note documents the initial prompt corpus and regression harness design for onboarding code generation and refactoring models. Focus areas: compilation-first correctness, unit-test-driven refactors, and style/linters enforcement. This is a working doc — contains dataset slices, representative prompts, evaluation signals, and an initial CI integration plan.

Scope and goals:
- Create a compact yet high-signal prompt corpus for validating new model variants before they are allowed into production runtimes.
- Prioritize artifacts that map cleanly to automated metrics: compile success, unit test pass rate, linter/style score, and semantic equivalence (where applicable).
- Make the harness small enough to run on pre-merge CI for model rollouts, but extensible for nightly/full regression runs.

Dataset composition (high level):
- Seed repos (30): small real-world toy repos and internal reference microservices with known test suites and CI configs. Repos chosen to cover: Python (3.10+) services, TypeScript/Node, and one small Java service to test multi-language behavior.
- Prompt families:
  * Compile-repair prompts (35 examples): short snippets that intentionally break build (missing import, syntax error, type mismatch). Expected signal: model returns corrected code that compiles with no additional human edits.
  * Unit-guided refactor prompts (40 examples): present a failing unit test + implementation, ask model to refactor to satisfy tests while preserving public API. Expected: unit test pass rate after applying patch.
  * Style-conformance prompts (25 examples): introduce stylistic violations (naming, spacing, docstring absence) and ask model to refactor to project linter rules. Expected: pass flake/ESLint with configured rule set and no functional regressions.
  * Test-oracle synthesis prompts (20 examples): supply function signature + spec, ask model to generate unit tests that catch edge cases. Expected: generated tests cover edge cases and run without false failures.
  * Regression traps (10 examples): intentionally ambiguous instructions / conflicting constraints to measure model robustness and fallback behavior.

Representative prompts (short samples):
- Compile-repair (Python):
  """
  File: utils/parse_config.py
  Content: def load(cfg_path):
      with open(cfgpath) as f:
          return json.load(f)
  Task: Fix the code so it loads the JSON config at cfg_path and include a brief one-line explanation.
  """
  Success signal: file fixes variable name, imports json, and function runs in REPL.

- Unit-guided refactor (TypeScript):
  """
  Given this failing test (tests/math.test.ts) and current implementation (src/math.ts), refactor src/math.ts to be more modular and make the test pass. Keep the exported function names identical. Explain changes in <= 3 lines.
  """
  Success signal: npm test returns green on that package.

- Style-conformance (Python):
  """
  Apply project style rules (black/flake8-ish subset: line length 88, snake_case for functions, typed function signatures). Return only the patched file content.
  """
  Success signal: linter exit code 0 and unit tests unchanged.

Evaluation metrics and thresholds (CI-friendly):
- compile_success_rate: percent of compile-repair prompts where patched repo builds in a clean container (threshold for onboarding: >= 85% for nightly, >= 92% for pre-release gate).
- unit_test_pass_rate: percent of unit-guided refactor prompts where the repo's test suite passes after applying model-generated patch (gate: >= 90% for canary, >= 96% for promoted).
- style_adherence_score: normalized score from linters (0-100). Expected improvement or parity vs baseline; gate: no net decrease in style score for critical rules.
- semantic_regression_count: number of human-verified semantic regressions found in sample (target: 0 for promoted models).
- tokens_per_fix and latency_ms: cost signals to monitor performance regressions.
- flaky_test_rate: percentage of generated tests that are nondeterministic under 10 runs (target: < 2%).

Regression harness design:
- Lightweight CI job (pre-merge): run a 5-example smoke subset (one per family) with strict timeouts (3m per example).
- Nightly full run: run the entire corpus in a k8s job with caching to avoid rebuilds; produce per-prompt artifacts (patch, diff, logs).
- Artifact storage: store patched files, test logs, linter outputs, and docker build logs in S3 with a structured prefix: s3://redwood-evals/code-onboarding/{model}/{run_ts}/.
- Result artifacts to be surfaced in a simple HTML report and an ML-specific dashboard (linked via GH status checks).

CI integration points and automation:
- bench-runner: small Go/Python runner (prototype exists in PR 88) that checks out seed repo, applies model patch (from model API), runs build/test/lint in an ephemeral container, captures exit codes and timing.
- GitHub status checks used for quick-canary results; include compact summary and link to full artifacts.
- Jira automation: failures above thresholds create ENG-automated tickets and attach the failing diff + logs.

Labeling and human review process:
- Auto-accept: if model meets all gated thresholds for the smoke subset, label as canary-ready.
- Human spot-check: 6 randomly sampled diffs per run reviewed by an engineer to catch semantic regressions that automated tests miss.
- Escalation: any human-verified semantic regression marks the model as rollback candidate and triggers deeper bisecting runs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Corpus diversity: we currently underweight asynchronous patterns and modern frameworks (FastAPI, Next.js). Need to add 8 more repo seeds. Owner: Marco.
- Type-level correctness: how to automatically detect subtle API contract breaks in the absence of exhaustive tests? Investigate property-based testing integration.
- Large-patch policy: define when to reject patches that replace >X% of file content (current heuristics: 40% threshold).
- Non-determinism: standardize retry policy vs marking as flaky.

Operational notes and pitfalls we've observed in prototypes:
- Models sometimes produce correct logic but forget to update import lists; include an import-check step in the harness.
- Over-aggressive formatting (reformat entire file) makes diffs noisy; capture normalized diffs using clang-format/black to reduce noise.
- Generated tests occasionally assert implementation details rather than behavior; prefer behavioral or property-based expectations when feasible.

Appendix: example CI summary output (compact):
- model: model-x-v3
- run_ts: 2026-03-01T04:12Z
- smoke_set: 5/5 passed
- compile_success_rate: 92%
- unit_test_pass_rate: 88% (2 failures: TS-refactor-07, Py-refactor-04)
- style_adherence_score: 98
- tokens_per_fix: median 420
- report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/redwood-evals/code-onboarding/model-x-v3/20260301/report.html

Contact / ownership:
- Corpus owner: Aisha Patel (eng-applied-ml)
- Automation/runner: Samira Khan (eng-platform)
- CI/Infra integration: Ethan Brooks (eng-sre)

If this looks reasonable we should:
1) merge the prototype runner PR and wire the 5-smoke CI job to model-onboarding repo.
2) add 8 more seed repos covering async + frameworks.
3) schedule 1-hour sync with product and devex to align gating thresholds and alerting.

Notes to self (scratch):
- Consider adding a small JS-only corpus for package managers (pnpm) to catch dependency resolution fixes.
- Track cost impact: compare tokens_per_fix * avg_token_cost to estimate model rollout cost for batch remediation flows.

End of doc.
